sources.title: Birnirk National Historic Landmark
sources.note: NPS site account of Piġniq, Birnirk chronology, houses, caches, food, tools, a preserved umiak and its relationship to later Thule archaeology and Iñupiat history.

sources.title: Wales Sites National Historic Landmark
sources.note: NPS history of the first systematically studied Alaskan Thule material, Birnirk-to-Thule stratigraphy and the changing interpretations built from harpoons and ceramics.

sources.title: Gambell Sites National Historic Landmark
sources.note: NPS synthesis of Saint Lawrence Island archaeological phases, winter houses, middens, burials and the research history of maritime traditions.

sources.title: Analyzing Early Driftwood Houses of Coastal Alaska
sources.note: NPS archaeology of driftwood movement, semi-subterranean houses, carpentry, permafrost preservation and Cape Espenberg construction change.

sources.title: Capturing History in the Beach Ridges of Cape Krusenstern
sources.note: NPS explanation of beach-ridge chronology, western Thule houses, settlement change and coastal erosion threats.

sources.title: Archeology at Katmai National Park
sources.note: NPS regional account of seasonal Thule settlements in southwest Alaska and the limits of artifact collecting without context.

sources.title: Thule: Ancient Whaling Traditions
sources.note: Iñupiat Heritage Center and NPS summary of northern and western Alaskan whaling, artistry, trade and rapid Arctic settlement.

sources.title: Culture and History at Auyuittuq National Park
sources.note: Parks Canada regional synthesis of early Thule food, seasonal travel, dogs, sleds, boats, winter houses, lamps and later Inuit continuity.

sources.title: Cultural History at Aulavik National Park
sources.note: Parks Canada explanation of archaeological culture labels, Banks Island Thule sites, bowhead economies and later Inuinnait connections.

sources.title: Kettle Lake Walking Tour
sources.note: Parks Canada guide to High Arctic Thule fox traps, dog sledding, qulliq lamps, snow knives, semi-subterranean houses and sea-ice camping.

sources.title: Of Young Caribou and Old Spirits
sources.note: Parks Canada account of stone food caches, radiocarbon limits, repeated inland use and research with Inuvialuit knowledge holders.

sources.title: Qajartalik, Nunavik
sources.note: Parks Canada account of a Dorset rock-marking site and chronology, used to keep Dorset material and Thule archaeology distinct.

sources.title: Thule Culture in Greenland
sources.note: National Museum of Denmark research overview of Greenland site distribution, whaling cooperation, settlement forms, exchange and archaeological study.

sources.title: Thule Snow Knife
sources.note: Canadian Museum of History catalog record for a circa 1400-or-later whale-bone, ivory and sinew construction tool.

sources.title: Bridport Inlet Archaeological Survey
sources.note: Canadian Museum of History archive record for Thule tent features, hearths, temporary camps and a radiocarbon result on Melville Island.

sources.title: The Walakpa Site, Alaska
sources.note: Smithsonian Libraries record of a deeply stratified Birnirk and Thule site, artifact phases and a historically important, revisable interpretation.

sources.title: The Timing of the Thule Migration
sources.note: Peer-reviewed radiocarbon study supporting a rapid thirteenth-century eastward migration from two western Canadian Arctic sites.

sources.title: The Earliest Thule Migration
sources.note: Canadian Archaeological Association article on small, rapid movements toward Lancaster Sound and the danger of climate-deterministic stories.

sources.title: The Organization of Production in Prehistoric Thule Whaling Societies
sources.note: Peer-reviewed artifact study of Classic Thule whaling households, production, cooperation and possible social differentiation in the central Canadian Arctic.

sources.title: Prehistoric Inuit Whalers Affected Arctic Freshwater Ecosystems
sources.note: Peer-reviewed lake-sediment research tracing nutrient changes from whale processing, refuse and settlement beside a central Arctic pond.

sources.title: Thule Winter Site Demography in the High Arctic
sources.note: Peer-reviewed warning that imposing house ruins may exaggerate how many people lived simultaneously at a winter site.

sources.title: Life Around the North Water Ecosystem
sources.note: Interdisciplinary research on changing whaling organization, settlement size, resource use and social continuity around the North Water polynya.

sources.title: The Sea Ice Never Stops
sources.note: Inuit Circumpolar Council report based on living Inuit hunters’ knowledge of sea-ice travel, safety, change and intergenerational learning; used only as labeled comparison.

sources.title: Bowhead Whale
sources.note: NOAA biology of bowhead blubber, ice-breaking skulls, baleen feeding, seasonal ice habitat and later commercial-whaling impacts.

sources.title: Paleoproteomic Identification of Fourteenth-Century Gut-Skin Garments
sources.note: Peer-reviewed proteomic research on Nuulliit clothing materials, conservation limits and early Greenland Thule households.

sources.title: Early Thule Winter Houses: An Archaeoentomological Analysis
sources.note: Peer-reviewed analysis of human lice distributions in four Greenland winter houses and cautious evidence for localized delousing practices.

sources.title: Qilakitsormiut
sources.note: Greenland National Museum account of the circa 1475 Qilakitsoq burials, family relationships, clothing, tattoos, amulets and belief.

sources.title: The Thule Inuit Mummies from Greenland
sources.note: Peer-reviewed review of Qilakitsoq and other Greenland mummies, soot exposure, parasites, clothing, childhood and interpretive limits.

sources.title: The Thule
sources.note: Memorial University heritage synthesis of Thule sewing tools, tailored clothing, hunting technology and regional archaeological evidence.

sources.title: An Archaeological View of the Thule and Inuit Occupation of Labrador
sources.note: Memorial University archaeological report on Labrador chronology, household objects, combs, needles, clothing fragments, dolls and miniatures.

sources.title: Culture and History at Ivvavik National Park
sources.note: Parks Canada regional history of Beaufort Sea driftwood houses, net fishing, communal beluga hunting and Inuvialuit continuity.

sources.title: Inuktut Qaliujaaqpait
sources.note: Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami history of much later missionary-era writing systems and Inuit-led modern orthography work, supporting the no-ancient-sample decision.

sources.title: Inuit Circumpolar Council International
sources.note: Inuit-led institutional source for living peoples, contemporary representation and circumpolar continuity, not an ancient-state analogy.

sources.title: Geoarchaeological Investigations at Sandhavn, South Greenland
sources.note: Antiquity project report on Norse and Indigenous landscape archaeology and the fragmentary evidence for interaction in southern Greenland.

sources.title: Thule Culture
sources.note: University of Alaska Museum overview of maritime tools, floats, houses, clothing, caches and cautiously interpreted armor evidence.

proposedOverrides.summary: Archaeological Thule tradition and diverse ancestral Inuit histories, not classical literary Thule, one state or a frozen culture.

batchIdentityNotes: The imported summary describes the unrelated classical Greek and Roman literary place Thule and is rejected for this archaeological record.
The coverage ledger calls the target a state, but archaeological Thule is a scholarly material-tradition label rather than a polity, self-name or uniform culture.
The 800 to 1200 target geometry is a southern Alaska polygon that omits tested northern origins and migration sites; it is audited but not treated as authoritative cultural territory.
The 1279, 1300 and 1400 files each contain two separate exact-id features: a large Arctic multipolygon and a duplicated southern Alaska polygon.
The 1492 target is a Greenland remnant; a broad 13-part Arctic feature returns at 1500 and vanishes at 1530. These are atlas taxonomy seams, not population events.
Birnirk, Punuk, Dorset and regional Thule variants remain archaeological classifications; living Inuit peoples and languages remain distinct.
Later Inuit knowledge is labeled comparison and belongs to living knowledge holders rather than being projected unchanged backward.
Contemporaneous written-language sample: none is securely attributable. Classical text, Norse runes and later Inuktut writing are not borrowed.
